title: Fine-tuning Gemma 3 1B for Luganda: from 0.06 to 13.85 BLEU
dek: QLoRA on a single T4 GPU turns a model with essentially no working Luganda into a functional bidirectional translator, using data derived almost entirely from one source.

sections.heading: The problem
paragraphs: Gemma 3 1B Instruct, like most general-purpose small LLMs, has almost no working knowledge of Luganda out of the box: 0.06 BLEU and 8.84 chrF++ on our English→Luganda eval, indistinguishable from random output. Luganda has roughly 5+ million speakers in Uganda, but the training data mainstream LLMs see for it is vanishingly small compared to English, French, or Swahili.

The question was whether a single consumer-GPU fine-tuning run could close meaningful ground here, given that the largest clean parallel corpus we could find was a fraction of the size typically used for high-resource language pairs.

sections.heading: Data
paragraphs: We built 94,542 training examples from roughly 24,000 clean English–Luganda parallel sentence pairs, drawn primarily from the Sunbird SALT dataset, a professionally translated, multi-way parallel corpus covering agriculture, health, society, and other locally relevant topics. Each pair was expanded into three task types: English→Luganda translation, Luganda→English translation, and open Luganda conversation, then split 90/5/5 into train/validation/test.

sections.heading: Method
paragraphs: QLoRA: a 4-bit NF4-quantized base model with LoRA adapters (rank 16, alpha 32, dropout 0.05) on the attention and MLP projections, trained for a single epoch with an effective batch size of 16, cosine learning rate schedule at 2e-4, and bf16 precision on a single Kaggle T4. The whole run (5,500+ steps) took about 8 hours and produced a 13.05M-parameter adapter, roughly 52 MB on disk.
Training and validation loss tracked each other closely throughout (2.07/2.01 at step 500 down to 1.24/1.26 by step 5000), with no sign of overfitting by the time training stopped.

sections.heading: What we'd try next
paragraphs: The model was trained for a single epoch on data covering agriculture, health, and society topics; both loss curves were still trending down when training stopped. Further epochs and additional sources (JW300, the Kimera corpus) would likely push scores higher, and Luganda→English quality specifically has room to close the gap with the reverse direction, since the base model's English fluency doesn't carry over as directly.

card.title: Adapting Gemma 3 1B for Luganda translation

title: Continued pretraining before translation: the Swahili-Gemma-1B recipe
dek: Swahili isn't as underrepresented as Luganda, but a two-stage pipeline (teach the model to read Swahili first, then teach it to translate) still meaningfully outperformed going straight to instruction tuning.

sections.heading: Two stages
paragraphs: We split the work in two. Stage 1 continues pretraining the base model on unlabeled Swahili text (JamiiForums-2B, a large monolingual Swahili forum corpus, and Inkuba-Mono, a Swahili monolingual dataset) with no instruction format at all, just raw next-token prediction. That produces an intermediate checkpoint that reads Swahili more fluently before it ever sees a translation pair.

Stage 2 is where translation ability is actually taught: QLoRA fine-tuning (rank 32, alpha 64, dropout 0.05) on top of the CPT checkpoint, for 3 epochs at a 2e-4 cosine schedule, effective batch size 32, packed to 512-token blocks. The adapter was then merged into full fp16 weights, the form the released model ships in.

sections.heading: Data
paragraphs: 159,311 examples after quality filtering: 32,414 from MAFAND-MT (human-translated news, via Masakhane), 58,052 from Rogendo's English-Swahili sentence pairs, 23,947 from Sunbird SALT, 29,991 from Inkuba-Swahili-MMT, plus smaller instruction-following sets (359 from Cohere's Aya dataset and 14,844 from Alpaca-cleaned-Swahili) so the model picks up general Swahili instruction-following alongside translation. That's 25,452 packed training blocks, roughly 13 million training tokens, over 2,388 steps and about 9 hours 45 minutes on a single T4.

One thing that didn't work: we planned to add back-translated monolingual Swahili (via NLLB) to the mix, but the monolingual source returned zero usable lines in this run; that augmentation simply didn't contribute to the released model, and we're noting it here.

title: Purpose-built beats general-purpose: NLLB LoRA vs. instruction-tuned LLMs for Swahili
dek: A small LoRA adapter on Meta's translation-specific NLLB-200 outscored every instruction-tuned chat model we compared it against on the same benchmark, including some many times its size.

sections.heading: Why try a non-chat architecture
paragraphs: Every other CommonMind model so far has been a fine-tuned instruction-tuned LLM (Gemma 3). NLLB-200 is a different kind of model entirely: an encoder-decoder architecture with a SentencePiece tokenizer, built by Meta specifically for translation across 200 languages, with no chat template and no general-purpose reasoning ability to spare. The question: does specializing the architecture, on top of the training data, buy anything on top of what instruction-tuned LLMs already achieve?

sections.heading: Method
paragraphs: LoRA (rank 16, alpha 32) on facebook/nllb-200-distilled-1.3B and facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M, trained one direction only, English→Swahili (eng_Latn→swh_Latn), on 145,707 parallel pairs: all of MAFAND-MT (32,414) and Sunbird SALT (23,947), plus Rogendo capped at 60,000 and Inkuba-Swahili-MMT capped at 30,000. 3 epochs, 3e-5 learning rate, effective batch size 32, max sequence length 128, on a single Kaggle T4, about 13,662 steps per model.

One honest wrinkle: raw training loss for both runs plateaued far higher (roughly 10–12) than the causal-LM losses we typically see finishing around 1.2–1.5 on our Gemma fine-tunes. That reflects a different loss landscape: NLLB's ~256K-token vocabulary changes what the raw cross-entropy number means, which is why we evaluate held-out translation quality directly.

sections.heading: How it stacks up
paragraphs: Scored on the same FLORES-200 devtest split (1,012 sentence pairs) used across our Swahili benchmarks, the 1.3B NLLB adapter reached 38.74 BLEU / 63.37 chrF++, and the 600M variant reached 35.97 / 61.26. Both beat Crane AI Labs' Swahili-Gemma-1B (27.6 / 56.8), Gemma 3 27B (29.4 / 60.0), and GPT-5 Mini (31.8 / 62.4) on the same benchmark, and the 1.3B model edges past Gemini 2.0 Flash (35.6 BLEU) too. The full comparison, with every source linked, is on the benchmarks page.
Neither model was trained or evaluated on the reverse direction (Swahili→English); that's untested and not claimed.

tagline: A Gemma 3 1B Instruct model adapted using QLoRA for English to Luganda and Luganda to English translation
overview: Built on Google's Gemma 3 1B Instruct architecture, this model uses QLoRA fine-tuning to improve English-to-Luganda and Luganda-to-English translation. It was trained primarily on the Sunbird SALT parallel corpus, covering agriculture, health, and society, adapting the base model with just 13.05 million trainable parameters in a 52 MB adapter that runs on consumer GPUs.
capabilities: Educational tools for Luganda language learning
achievements: BLEU 13.85 on the held-out English↔Luganda test split, up from 0.06 on the base model
chrF++ 46.59 strong character level accuracy for morphologically rich Luganda
Only 52 MB adapter on top of the 1B base model
Runs on consumer GPUs with QLoRA (4-bit quantization and LoRA adapters)

usage.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer, BitsAndBytesConfig
from peft import PeftModel
import torch

base_model_id = "google/gemma-3-1b-it"
adapter_id = "AmplifiedAccess/Luganda-gemma-1b-it"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(base_model_id)

model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(
    base_model_id,
    quantization_config=BitsAndBytesConfig(
        load_in_4bit=True,
        bnb_4bit_quant_type="nf4",
        bnb_4bit_compute_dtype=torch.bfloat16,
    ),
    device_map={"": 0},
)
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(model, adapter_id)
model.eval()

# Translate civic content English → Luganda
prompt = "Translate to Luganda:\nA community officer can help residents complete forms, check eligibility, and even process applications offline."
messages = [{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
inputs = tokenizer.apply_chat_template(
    messages, return_tensors="pt", return_dict=True, add_generation_prompt=True
).to(model.device)

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=128, do_sample=False)

prompt_len = inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]
response = tokenizer.decode(outputs[0][prompt_len:], skip_special_tokens=True).strip()
print(response)

tagline: A Gemma 3 1B model adapted using LoRA for English to Swahili translation
overview: Built on Google's Gemma 3 1B architecture, this model uses LoRA fine-tuning to improve English-to-Swahili translation. It was trained on more than 159,000 examples from MAFAND-MT, Sunbird SALT, Rogendo, Inkuba-Swahili-MMT, Aya, and Alpaca-Swahili, adapting the base model with just 26.09 million trainable parameters merged into full weights.
achievements: BLEU 28.86 on English to Swahili (FLORES-200 devtest), up from 0.41 on the base model
chrF++ 54.77, up from 14.28 on the base model
26.09M trainable LoRA parameters, merged into a 1B model
Quantized to ~814MB for CPU/consumer hardware via Ollama

usage.code:
from transformers import AutoModelForCausalLM, AutoTokenizer
import torch

model_id = "AmplifiedAccess/Swahili-gemma-1b-it"
tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(model_id)
model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained(model_id, dtype=torch.float16, device_map="auto")

prompt = ("<start_of_turn>user\n"
          "Translate the following English sentence to Swahili.\n"
          "English: The children are playing outside.\nSwahili:<end_of_turn>\n"
          "<start_of_turn>model\n")

inputs = tokenizer(prompt, return_tensors="pt").to(model.device)
with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, max_new_tokens=128, do_sample=False)

response = tokenizer.decode(outputs[0][inputs["input_ids"].shape[1]:], skip_special_tokens=True)
print(response.strip())

tagline: An NLLB-200 1.3B model adapted using LoRA for English to Swahili translation
overview: Built on Meta's NLLB-200 1.3B architecture, this model uses LoRA fine-tuning to improve English-to-Swahili translation. It was trained on more than 145,000 parallel sentence pairs from MAFAND-MT, Sunbird SALT, Rogendo, and Inkuba-Swahili-MMT, adapting the base model with just 23.6 million trainable parameters.
achievements: BLEU 38.74 / chrF++ 63.37 on FLORES devtest, beating the CraneAILabs Swahili-Gemma-1B reference (27.6 BLEU / 56.8 chrF++)
Only 23.6M trainable LoRA parameters, ~1.7% of the 1.37B base model

usage.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import PeftModel

base_model_id = "facebook/nllb-200-distilled-1.3B"
adapter_id = "AmplifiedAccess/Swahili-nllb-1.3b"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(base_model_id, src_lang="eng_Latn")
model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(base_model_id)
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(model, adapter_id)
model.eval()

text = "A community officer can help residents complete forms, check eligibility, and even process applications offline."
inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")
target_lang_id = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("swh_Latn")

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, forced_bos_token_id=target_lang_id, max_new_tokens=128)

print(tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)[0])

tagline: An NLLB-200 600M model adapted using LoRA for English to Swahili translation
overview: Built on Meta's NLLB-200 600M architecture, this model uses LoRA fine-tuning to improve English-to-Swahili translation. It was trained on the same corpus mix as Swahili-nllb-1.3B, drawn from MAFAND-MT, Sunbird SALT, Rogendo, and Inkuba-Swahili-MMT, adapting the base model with just 8.65 million trainable parameters for tighter hardware budgets.
achievements: BLEU 35.97 / chrF++ 61.26 on FLORES devtest, beating the CraneAILabs Swahili-Gemma-1B reference (27.6 BLEU / 56.8 chrF++) at under half the parameters
Only 8.65M trainable LoRA parameters, ~1.4% of the 615M base model
Runs on more constrained hardware than the 1.3B variant

usage.code:
import torch
from transformers import AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM, AutoTokenizer
from peft import PeftModel

base_model_id = "facebook/nllb-200-distilled-600M"
adapter_id = "AmplifiedAccess/Swahili-nllb-600m"

tokenizer = AutoTokenizer.from_pretrained(base_model_id, src_lang="eng_Latn")
model = AutoModelForSeq2SeqLM.from_pretrained(base_model_id)
model = PeftModel.from_pretrained(model, adapter_id)
model.eval()

text = "A community officer can help residents complete forms, check eligibility, and even process applications offline."
inputs = tokenizer(text, return_tensors="pt")
target_lang_id = tokenizer.convert_tokens_to_ids("swh_Latn")

with torch.no_grad():
    outputs = model.generate(**inputs, forced_bos_token_id=target_lang_id, max_new_tokens=128)

print(tokenizer.batch_decode(outputs, skip_special_tokens=True)[0])

You may provide information when you:

contribute to research or community initiatives;
request access to particular resources; or
use developer tools that require authentication.
This may include your name, email address, organisation, account information, and information you choose to include in communications with us.

maintain accounts and developer access;

understand how the platform is used;

evaluate and improve models, datasets, benchmarks, and tools;
conduct research;

We do not use personal information for purposes unrelated to CommonMind without an appropriate basis.
Civic Language Data and Research
CommonMind develops infrastructure for understanding civic speech across languages.

Datasets, research resources, models, and benchmarks published through the platform may have their own documentation describing their sources, collection methods, intended uses, licenses, limitations, and relevant privacy considerations.

Information intentionally submitted to public repositories or public contribution channels may become publicly available.
